Before starting the experimental trials, participants did 20 practice trials in which feedback was included. After the WM phase, participants completed a two-minute filler phase in which they were presented with several mathematical problems. Participants were instructed to solve as many problems as possible within the two-minute timeframe by typing their response using the keyboard. Following the filler phase, participants were presented with the LTM test. On each LTM trial, two images were presented side by side, and participants were asked which of the images they remembered from the WM phase. To respond, participants were instructed to click on one of the images. The LTM test included 200 trials with an equal division of trials per probe type: 50 cued-tested, 50 cued-untested, 50 uncued-tested, and 50 uncued-untested. Feedback was presented for 500ms after each response in the LTM test.

In Experiments 1 and 2, before starting the experiment, half of the participants were explicitly told that the memory items of the WM phase would be tested in an LTM test at the end of the experiment, regardless of whether the item was cued or not in the working memory phase. In Experiment 3, there were three groups of participants: one group was unaware of the upcoming LTM test (like in Experiments 1 and 2), one group was informed about the upcoming LTM test (again, like in Experiments 1 and 2), and one group was informed about the upcoming LTM test and told that they would receive a financial reward (£4) if they performed better than the average of a similar group of participants that had done the same test (based on Experiment 1, this was set to 73%). This award was paid out as announced.

Analysis

All analyses were done using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2021; v2026.01.1). For all experiments included in this study, we preregistered to perform the same analytical steps. For all experiments, steps 1 to 3 included Prioritization Status as a within-subjects variable and Test Awareness as a between-subjects variable, and step 4 included the full experimental design. To evaluate the Bayes Factors, we used the classification according to Lee and Wagenmakers (2014).

In Step 1, we preregistered to assess whether prioritization (i.e., the retro-cue) benefits WM performance in both Test Awareness groups. For this purpose, we computed Bayesian logistic mixed-effects models on the accuracy data of the WM trials with a WM test. In Step 2, to investigate our main hypothesis that attention in WM benefits LTM more when participants are aware of the upcoming LTM test than when they are unaware, we preregistered to compute Bayesian logistic mixed-effects models on the accuracy data of the LTM test for the untested WM items. In Step 3, we preregistered to examine whether attention in WM also benefits LTM performance more when people are aware of the upcoming LTM test when the memory items were also tested in WM, using the same statistical model as for Step 2. In Step 4, we computed not preregistered Bayesian logistic mixed-effects models on the full experimental design to establish the overall evidence for or against cueing effects (Prioritization Status) and testing effects (WM Test) in each experiment.

Results

Working Memory Performance

The results are presented in Table 1. For all experiments, we replicated the typically observed retro-cue benefit in WM (Souza & Oberauer, 2016). Participants were more accurate when the tested item had been prioritized compared to when it was unprioritized (see Figure 2). This confirms that participants used the cue to focus attention on this item in WM. Working Memory Performance for Experiment 1 (left), 2 (middle), and 3 (right). Note. Graph presented with standard error of the mean bars and individual scores (grey).

Long-Term Memory Performance: Untested WM items

LTM performance for the WM items that were not tested in the WM phase provides the purest test of whether focused attention benefits LTM unconfounded by the WM test. The results are again presented in Table 1. In Experiment 1, we observed anecdotal evidence against the main effect of Prioritization Status. In contrast, in Experiments 2 and 3, we observed strong evidence (BFs > 10) in favor of this main effect. In these experiments, participants performed better on the LTM test for items that had been prioritized in WM compared to items that were unprioritized (see Fig. 3). Furthermore, we observed moderate to strong evidence (BF01 > 7) against the main effect of Test Awareness. In Experiments 1 and 3, we also observed moderate to strong evidence (BF01 > 8) against the interaction between Test Awareness and Prioritization Status. In Experiment 2, the evidence for this interaction remained anecdotal. Thus, performance on the LTM test did not credibly differ regardless of whether participants were aware of the LTM test or not. Additionally, the benefit of focused attention in WM on LTM performance did not change with respect to participants' awareness of the LTM test. Note. Graph presented with standard error of the mean bars and individual scores (grey).

Long-Term Memory Performance: Tested WM items

For the tested WM items, we only observed strong evidence for the main effect of Prioritization Status in Experiment 2 (see Table 1). In Experiment 1, we observed moderate evidence against this main effect, and in Experiment 3, the evidence remained anecdotal.

Performance was better for the prioritized WM items than the unprioritized WM items in Experiment 2 (see Fig. 4). For all experiments, we observed moderate evidence (BF01 > 6) against the main effect of Test Awareness and strong evidence (BF01 > 14) against the interaction between Test Awareness and Prioritization Status. Thus, like for the untested WM items, LTM performance did not differ regardless of whether participants were aware of the LTM test or not, and this also did not interact with the prioritization status of the WM items. Note. Graph presented with standard error of the mean bars and individual scores (grey).

Long-Term Memory Performance: Three-Way Analysis

The three-way analysis demonstrated that, overall, there is strong evidence that focused attention in WM benefits LTM in Experiments 2 and 3 (see Table 1). However, the size of this benefit remained modest (see Fig. 5). Additionally, all three experiments showed extreme evidence (BFs > 100) for a testing effect in WM on LTM performance. Performance was consistently better for WM items that had been tested in WM compared to items that had not been tested (see Fig. 5). In line with our previous analyses, none of the experiments displayed any evidence in favor of a main effect of Test Awareness. Furthermore, there was also no evidence in favor of any of the two-way interactions or the three-way interaction. Note. Benefit values represent the difference in performance (e.g., average LTM performance for cued WM items minus average LTM performance for uncued WM items). Graph presented with standard error of the mean bars and individual scores (grey).

General Discussion

We investigated whether the effect of focused attention during WM maintenance on LTM performance depends on an intent to remember the information for later purposes. We hypothesized that when people intend to remember, they might use the opportunity to focus attention more strategically by making use of maintenance strategies such as elaboration or refreshing. We obtained evidence against this hypothesis. Focused attention in WM did not interact with intentionality to improve LTM performance. Furthermore, our findings showed that focused attention during WM maintenance indeed benefits LTM (Experiments 2 and 3), but that this benefit is small and inconsistent, in line with the mixed findings in previous literature (Hautekiet & Oberauer, 2026). We observed no evidence for a main effect of Test Awareness, speaking against a contribution of the intention to remember for LTM formation.

Even when participants were explicitly incentivized to perform well on the LTM test, performance did not improve (Experiment 3). Furthermore, while not the focus of the current study, our findings demonstrated a relatively large and robust WM-based testing effect. LTM performance was substantially improved when the information had been tested within the WM phase, compared to when it had not been tested. We will discuss each of these results in more detail below.

Focused attention and intentionality do not interact to improve LTM

Our findings showed no interaction between focused attention and the intent to remember information for later for improvement of LTM. While the current study was the first to look at the interaction between attention and intention using a direct measure of attention (i.e., retro-cue), Labaronne et al. (2024) examined how intentions modulate the effect of attention in WM on LTM performance using an indirect measure of attention. To manipulate attention, Labaronne and colleagues varied the free time during a complex-span test and relied on the assumption that people use that time to spontaneously refresh information in WM. Like in the current study, Labaronne and colleagues made one group of participants aware of the LTM test whereas the other group remained unaware. In line with the current findings, Labaronne et al. observed no convincing evidence for the interaction between attention in WM and intentionality or for the main effect of intentionality. In a follow-up experiment, Labaronne et al. used reward for prioritization by making some items worth more points when recalled correctly (within-subjects) and manipulated the intention to remember items over the long term by varying whether immediate or delayed recall would be rewarded (between-subjects). Here, the authors observed that when delayed recall was incentivized, the long-term benefit for highvalue items became substantially larger than when immediate recall was incentivized. This suggests that participants were doing something differently during the WM task that impacted LTM performance. We did not see such increased attentional benefit for the aware-reward group (delayed memory test incentivized) in our Experiment 3. Thus, our findings align with Labaronne et al.'s first experiment, but not the second.

Focused attention in WM offers a small benefit for LTM

Whereas there was no interaction between attention and intentionality in WM, focused attention during WM maintenance did improve LTM in two of three experiments. Still, as illustrated in Figure 5, the size of the benefit remained rather modest, which aligns with our review of the literature (see Hautekiet & Oberauer, 2026).

Does this mean attention is not important for the creation of LTM? This conclusion would be premature. However, it is possible that attention is highly beneficial when directed to a perceived stimulus, because it serves to extract information that is added to the memory trace, whereas when it is directed to WM, attention cannot gain any information that has not already been encoded and thus, attention cannot strengthen the memory of an item.

The intent to remember does not impact LTM performance

Across three experiments, we did not observe an improvement in LTM when participants were aware of the delayed memory test or when they were financially incentivized to perform well on this delayed test. This aligns with a widespread literature that found that the intent to remember has no causal role in LTM formation (e.g., Craik & Tulving, 1975; Evans & Baddeley, 2018; Hyde & Jenkins, 1969 , 1973; Oberauer & Greve, 2022), but contrasts with past findings that did observe that the intent to remember matters for LTM (Loaiza & Souza, 2024; Popov & Dames, 2023). Popov and Dames (2023) suggested that this difference is due to design choices such that little to no difference in LTM performance will be observed when intentionality is manipulated between subjects, whereas a substantial boost in performance will be observed when it is manipulated within subjects. Additionally, they observed that intentional encoding can improve memory for content-context bindings while memory for individual items can still be retrieved under incidental encoding. In agreement with this, we used a betweensubjects design and tested memory for individual items, and we did not observe a difference in performance between intentional and incidental memory.

Alternatively, it is possible that we were simply not successful in manipulating intentionality. In real life, people's intent to remember something is often tied to personal or emotional value (e.g., studying for an exam, remembering a loved one's birthday). It is possible that simply telling participants about the LTM, as done in Experiments 1 and 2, does not induce a genuine intent to remember. In Experiment 3, we attempted to increase motivation by offering a financial reward based on LTM performance (£4 on top of £5.25 for participation). Here, again, it is possible that a financial reward was not sufficient to induce a genuine intent to remember, and that we were therefore unable to successfully manipulate intentionality.

Testing in WM benefits LTM

While not the focus of the current study, our findings convincingly demonstrated that testing in WM benefits LTM performance. The size of this benefit is larger than the benefit for attention in WM (see Figure 5). The presence of this testing benefit highlights the need to control for testing when investigating the role of attention in the WM-LTM transfer. Because previous studies have not consistently accounted for this (see Hautekiet and Oberauer, 2026), some reported attentional benefits in LTM performance may reflect testing benefits.

The presence of a testing benefit on top of an attentional benefit aligns with the findings by Sabo and Schneider (2025), who demonstrated that further retention of LTM representations benefits from focused attention and testing in WM. Furthermore, the observed testing benefit aligns with a large body of literature that showed that retrieval practice improves long-term retention (for reviews, see Roediger & Butler, 2011; Rowland, 2014). In this literature, the memory test is administered at least several minutes after encoding, which surpasses the window of WM storage. Thus, in this context, a testing benefit refers to an improvement in LTM performance after retrieval practice of information that has already been encoded in LTM. Our findings extend this testing effect such that testing improves LTM performance for newly encoded information in WM (see also e.g., Atkinson et al., 2024; Born & Spitzer, 2026; Sutterer & Awh, 2016; Xie & Reuter-Lorenz, 2024).

What remains unclear is why testing in WM benefits LTM. In the testing literature, it has been well-established that retrieval practice improves long-term retention beyond reexposure or restudying of the materials (e.g., Carpenter, 2009; Mulligan & Peterson, 2015; Roediger III & Karpicke, 2006; for a review, see Rowland, 2014). In our experiments, we observed a small benefit of retrieval without re-exposure (attentional benefit from cueing) and a substantial benefit of retrieval with re-exposure to the materials. The difference in the size of these effects could simply reflect a difference in exposure duration (once at encoding vs. both at encoding and at the WM test). Still, Xie and Reuter-Lorenz (2024) showed that having to make a choice at the WM test (e.g., choosing between three alternative-forced choice options) improves LTM more than the opportunity to restudy the materials. This suggests that there may be more to the WM testing benefit than a mere re-exposure effect.

Conclusion

This study examined whether focused attention in WM (as induced by cueing) interacts with the intention to remember (as induced through test awareness) in facilitating LTM formation. Across three experiments, the results provided evidence against the hypothesis. The awareness of an upcoming LTM test -which was assumed to induce an intent to rememberdid not result in improved LTM performance, even when performance on the LTM test was incentivized with a financial reward. Focused attention in WM via retro-cueing did yield a positive effect on LTM, however, this benefit remained small and did not occur in all experiments. In contrast, testing in WM produced a large, robust benefit on subsequent LTM retention. Overall, these findings indicate that while focusing attention in WM through retrocueing plays at best a minor, non-strategic role in LTM formation, active retrieval through WM testing has a more substantial impact on LTM formation.
